routes.name: Visa Waiver Program (ESTA)
routes.summary: Citizens of participating countries can visit the US for tourism or business for up to 90 days without a visa. You need an approved ESTA before you board.

other: Citizen or national of a country in the Visa Waiver Program. The official list is on the State Dept VWP page.
Passport must be valid 6 months past your planned departure, unless a country agreement says otherwise.
E-passport with a chip is required.
Must travel on an approved air or sea carrier.
A recent visa refusal can lead to ESTA denial or extra review.
Approval does not guarantee entry. A CBP officer decides at the port.

stay.note: No extension and no change of status. Short trips to Canada, Mexico or nearby islands count toward the 90 days.

routes.processing: CBP says approvals are usually valid for two years or until the passport expires, whichever is first. A new ESTA is needed for a new passport, name change or changed answers. ESTA fee amount not confirmed here, check the official site.

routes.name: Visa exemption for Canada and Bermuda citizens
routes.summary: Citizens of Canada and Bermuda generally do not need a nonimmigrant visa for tourism in the US.

other: Rules for length of stay and other purposes were not confirmed on the page. Check CBP at the border.

routes.name: B-2 Visitor Visa (Tourism)
routes.summary: Visa for tourism, visiting family and friends, and medical treatment. Needed unless you qualify for the Visa Waiver Program or are exempt.

other: Citizens of Visa Waiver Program countries can use ESTA instead.
Fee, length of stay and interview rules were not confirmed. Check the State Dept visitor visa page.

routes.name: B-1 Business Visitor Visa
routes.summary: For short business trips such as meetings, conferences, contract talks and short training. You must plan a limited stay and keep a home abroad.

other: Must show a residence abroad you do not plan to give up.
The USCIS page is inconsistent on the initial stay (up to 1 year in one place, a 6 month maximum in a table). Confirm with CBP at entry.

stay.note: Extensions can be requested in blocks of up to 6 months with Form I-539. USCIS says total time on one trip is generally up to 1 year.

routes.name: Transit Visa (C-1) and transit rules
routes.summary: A C visa covers travelers passing through the US to another country. Official rules on who needs one and on airside transit could not be confirmed.

other: The official transit visa page could not be opened. Check the State Dept transit page before relying on this.
The USCIS B-1 page lists transiting through the US as an allowed activity.

routes.name: H-1B Specialty Occupation Visa
routes.summary: Work visa for jobs that need at least a bachelor's degree or equivalent. Your US employer files a petition for you. Some categories have annual caps.

eligibility.education: Bachelor's degree or equivalent experience, tied to the job
other: H-1B and L applicants do not have to prove intent to return home.
Cap amounts and lottery rules were not confirmed here, check USCIS.

steps: Employer files Form I-129 with USCIS (some roles need a labor certification first).
After approval, apply for the visa at a US embassy or consulate if you are abroad.

routes.name: H-1B1 Specialty Occupation (Chile and Singapore)
routes.summary: Specialty occupation visa for citizens of Chile and Singapore. It is not petition-based. You apply through the embassy process.

other: Cap, duration and exact steps were not confirmed here.

routes.name: H-2A Temporary Agricultural Worker
routes.summary: Seasonal or temporary farm work for a US employer. Limited to citizens of designated countries, with narrow exceptions.

other: Only citizens of designated countries qualify. See the official list on USCIS.
Employer needs a temporary labor certification and an approved petition.

stay.note: Each extension is up to 1 year. After 3 years you must spend an uninterrupted 3 months outside the US before returning in H-2A. Earlier H or L time counts.

steps: Employer gets a temporary labor certification.
Worker applies for the visa abroad.

routes.name: H-2B Temporary Non-Agricultural Worker
routes.summary: Temporary or seasonal non-farm work for a US employer. Limited to citizens of designated countries, with narrow exceptions.

other: Employer needs approved petition and, in most cases, a labor certification.
Annual cap and stay limits were not confirmed here. Check USCIS.

routes.name: L-1 Intracompany Transferee
routes.summary: For managers, executives and specialized-knowledge employees moving to a related US office of their current employer.

other: The US entity must be a branch, parent, affiliate or subsidiary of your employer abroad.
You must have worked for that employer abroad for one year within the previous three years.
L and H-1B applicants do not have to prove intent to return home.
Maximum stay was not confirmed here.

routes.name: O-1 Extraordinary Ability
routes.summary: For people with extraordinary achievement in science, art, education, business or athletics, or a record of national or international acclaim in film and TV. Support staff can qualify too.

other: A US employer or agent files Form I-129.
Evidence criteria and stay length were not confirmed here. Check USCIS.

routes.name: E-1 Treaty Trader
routes.summary: For nationals of a treaty country who carry on substantial trade between the US and their country.

other: Must be a national of a treaty country. The treaty list is on the State Dept site.
The US business must be at least 50% owned by people of that nationality.
More than 50% of the business's international trade must be between the US and the treaty country.
Employees need an executive, supervisory or essential skills role.
You must intend to leave the US when your status ends.

sources.label: State Dept: Treaty Trader, Treaty Investor and E-3

routes.name: E-2 Treaty Investor
routes.summary: For nationals of a treaty country who invest a substantial amount in a real, operating US business and come to develop and direct it.

other: Must be a national of a treaty country.
The business must be at least 50% owned by treaty nationals, and you need at least 50% ownership or operational control.
The investment must be substantial and the business a real, non-marginal enterprise. Funds sitting in a bank account generally do not count.
Employees must share the owner's treaty nationality and hold executive, supervisory or essential skills roles.
No fixed dollar minimum was stated on these pages.
You must intend to leave the US when your status ends.

stay.note: Up to two years at a time, with no limit on the number of extensions.

routes.processing: Spouses in E-2 status are generally work authorized without a separate permit.

sources.label: State Dept: Treaty Trader, Treaty Investor and E-3

routes.name: E-3 Australian Specialty Occupation
routes.summary: Specialty occupation work visa for Australian citizens.

eligibility.education: Required academic qualifications, or equivalent education and experience
other: Employer must get an approved Labor Condition Application from the Department of Labor.
The job must meet the specialty occupation standard.
Spouse needs a marriage certificate. The US does not recognize de facto partners for this.
You must intend to leave the US when your status ends.

sources.label: State Dept: Treaty Trader, Treaty Investor and E-3

routes.name: TN USMCA Professional
routes.summary: For Canadian and Mexican citizens with a job offer in a profession on the USMCA list.

other: Must work in a USMCA-listed profession with a prearranged job. Self-employment is not allowed.
Permanent residents of Canada or Mexico do not qualify, only citizens.
Canadians normally apply at a port of entry with no visa. Mexicans need a TN visa.
Canadians living abroad bringing non-Canadian family need a TN visa so the family can get TD visas.

fees.label: TN visa application fee (as shown on State Dept page)

routes.name: F-1 Student Visa
routes.summary: For full-time study at a SEVP-approved US school, from universities to language programs. M visas cover vocational schools.

other: Must be accepted by a SEVP-approved school, get an I-20 and pay the SEVIS I-901 fee.
You cannot study on ESTA or a B visa, except short recreational non-credit courses.
Apply up to 365 days before the program starts. Enter no more than 30 days before.
Spouse and children living with you get their own I-20s but do not pay the SEVIS fee.

stay.note: Stay until the program end date on your I-20 plus 60 days, including any OPT period.

steps: Get accepted and receive Form I-20.
Apply for the visa and attend the interview.
Enter the US with your I-20.
routes.processing: Optional Practical Training needs an OPT-endorsed I-20 and an EAD from USCIS. Work must be directly related to your field of study.

routes.name: J-1 Exchange Visitor
routes.summary: For approved exchange programs such as students, researchers, interns and trainees. You need a program sponsor.

other: Needs a Form DS-2019 from an approved sponsor. Trainees and interns also need DS-7002.
You cannot use ESTA or a B visa for J-1 activities.
Two-year home-country rule applies if the program is government funded, you are in graduate medical training, or your country is on the Exchange Visitor Skills List. Waivers can be requested.
Enter no more than 30 days before your program starts.

fees.label: No visa fee for official US Government sponsored programs

routes.name: K-1 Fiance(e) Visa
routes.summary: A US citizen sponsors a fiance(e) to come to the US and marry within 90 days, then apply for a green card.

other: Both people must be legally free to marry.
You generally must have met in person within the past two years, unless USCIS grants an exception.
The US citizen files Form I-129F and later files an I-864 affidavit of support.

stay.note: Visa is valid for one entry within 6 months of issue. You must marry within 90 days of arriving.

steps: After approval the case goes to the embassy abroad.
Complete DS-160, medical exam and interview.
Enter the US and marry within 90 days.
File to adjust status to permanent resident.

routes.name: Family Green Card: Immediate Relatives of US Citizens
routes.summary: Spouses, unmarried children under 21, and parents of US citizens get a green card with no annual cap on visas.

other: Spouses and unmarried children under 21 of a US citizen qualify. Parents qualify if the citizen is 21 or older.
The citizen files Form I-130. If you are in the US you can file I-485 at the same time.
If you are abroad the case goes through the National Visa Center and a consulate.

fees.label: Immigrant visa application fee (immediate relative and family preference)

sources.label: State Dept: Fees for Visa Services

routes.name: Family Green Card: Family Preference Categories
routes.summary: Capped categories for more distant relatives of US citizens and certain relatives of green card holders. Expect waits for a visa number.

other: Petitioner must be at least 21 and a US citizen or green card holder.
US citizens can petition for a spouse, child, parent or sibling. Green card holders can petition for a spouse or unmarried child.
The sub-categories (F1 to F4) and current wait times were not confirmed. Check the monthly Visa Bulletin.

fees.label: Immigrant visa application fee (immediate relative and family preference)

routes.name: EB-1 Priority Workers
routes.summary: Green card for people with extraordinary ability, outstanding professors and researchers, and multinational managers and executives. No labor certification.

other: Extraordinary ability: sustained national or international acclaim, a major one-time award, or at least 3 of 10 evidence criteria. You can self-petition.
Professors and researchers: at least 3 years of experience, a permanent or tenure-track offer, and international recognition.
Multinational managers: 1 year in a managerial role abroad in the last 3 years with the same employer or affiliate, and a US employer in business for at least 1 year.
Employer files Form I-140 (self-petition allowed for extraordinary ability).

sources.label: State Dept: Fees for Visa Services

routes.name: EB-2 Advanced Degree or Exceptional Ability
routes.summary: Green card for advanced degree professionals and people with exceptional ability. Usually needs a labor certification, unless you get a national interest waiver.

eligibility.education: Advanced degree or equivalent, or exceptional ability
other: Employer files ETA-9089 with the Department of Labor, then Form I-140 within 180 days of approval.
A national interest waiver skips the labor certification. Its criteria were not confirmed here.

sources.label: State Dept: Fees for Visa Services

routes.name: EB-3 Professionals, Skilled and Other Workers
routes.summary: Green card for professionals with a bachelor's degree, skilled workers with 2 years of experience, and other workers. Usually needs a labor certification.

other: Professionals need a bachelor's degree.
Skilled workers need at least 2 years of experience.
Other workers have less than 2 years of experience, for jobs where qualified US workers are not available.
Employer files ETA-9089 and then Form I-140.

sources.label: State Dept: Fees for Visa Services

routes.name: EB-4 Certain Religious Workers
routes.summary: Green card for certain religious workers. Filed on Form I-360, and in some cases the worker can petition for themselves.

other: Other EB-4 special immigrant groups were not confirmed here.

routes.name: EB-5 Immigrant Investor
routes.summary: Green card for investors who put capital into a new commercial enterprise that creates at least 10 full-time US jobs.

other: Must create full-time jobs (35+ hours a week) for at least 10 qualifying workers. Regional center projects can count indirect jobs.
A lower amount applies in a targeted employment area (rural, or unemployment at least 150% of the national average).
Current investment amounts changed under the 2022 EB-5 Reform and Integrity Act. The page read was outdated, so no amount is listed here. Check USCIS.

sources.label: USCIS: About the EB-5 Visa Classification

routes.name: Diversity Visa Lottery (Green Card Lottery)
routes.summary: Annual lottery for a green card for people from countries with low US immigration. You need a high school education or qualifying work experience.

other: Principal applicant needs a 12-year formal education comparable to US high school (a GED does not count), or 2 years of work experience in the last 5 years in an occupation rated Job Zone 4 or 5 with SVP 7.0 or higher on O*NET.
Spouse and children do not need to meet these.
Eligible countries and entry dates change every year. They were not confirmed here. Check the State Dept DV page.

fees.label: Diversity Visa lottery visa fee (as shown on State Dept fee page)

sources.label: State Dept: Diversity Visa, Confirm Your Qualifications
State Dept: Fees for Visa Services

routes.name: Asylum
routes.summary: Protection for people in the US who fear persecution. Apply affirmatively with USCIS (Form I-589) or defensively in immigration court.

other: You must be physically in the US. You can apply regardless of how you arrived or your status.
You must apply within one year of your last arrival, with exceptions for changed or extraordinary circumstances.
Asylum applicants are not automatically authorized to work.

steps: File Form I-589 with USCIS, or request asylum in immigration court.
Attend an interview with an asylum officer (affirmative) or a hearing (defensive).

sources.label: USCIS: Obtaining Asylum in the United States

routes.name: Refugee Resettlement (USRAP)
routes.summary: You need a referral to the US Refugee Admissions Program first. If accepted, a USCIS officer interviews you abroad. No application fee.

other: Referral needed, for example from UNHCR, a US embassy or a designated NGO.
Approved refugees get a medical exam, cultural orientation and travel help with a travel loan.

routes.name: Green Card for Refugees
routes.summary: Refugees apply for a green card about one year after arriving in the US using Form I-485, with no filing or biometrics fee.

other: Must have entered the US as a refugee.

routes.name: Naturalization (5 years as green card holder)
routes.summary: Green card holders can apply for US citizenship after 5 years. You need basic English, a civics test and good moral character.

eligibility.language: Speak, read and write basic English. Some older long-term residents are exempt from the English test.
other: At least 5 years as a green card holder with continuous US residence.
At least 30 months physically in the US in those 5 years.
At least 3 months in the state or USCIS district where you apply.
Pass a civics test, show good moral character and attachment to the Constitution, and take the oath.

citizenship.note: The US does not make you choose and puts no limits on holding another citizenship. Your other country may have its own rules.

sources.label: USCIS: Naturalization as a Green Card holder of 5 years
USCIS: Continuous Residence and Physical Presence

routes.name: Naturalization (3 years, married to a US citizen)
routes.summary: Green card holders married to and living with a US citizen can apply after 3 years.

other: Green card holder for at least 3 years, married to and living with your US citizen spouse for those 3 years.
At least 18 months physically in the US in those 3 years, and 3 months in your state or district.
Pass a civics test, show good moral character, and take the oath.
Different rules apply if your citizen spouse works abroad for a qualifying US employer.

citizenship.note: The US does not make you choose another citizenship.

sources.label: USCIS: Naturalization as the spouse of a U.S. citizen
USCIS: Continuous Residence and Physical Presence

routes.name: Citizenship by Birth in the US
routes.summary: People born in the US and subject to its jurisdiction are citizens at birth, under long-standing statute. People born in American Samoa and Swains Island are generally nationals, not citizens.

other: There has been recent legal and policy action on birthright citizenship. The USCIS page read did not address it, so confirm the current rules before relying on this.
Births in some territories (for example Puerto Rico, Guam, US Virgin Islands) can also confer citizenship.

sources.label: USCIS Policy Manual: Born in the United States

routes.name: Citizenship by Descent (Born Abroad to a US Citizen)
routes.summary: A child born abroad can be a US citizen at birth if a parent was a US citizen and met the US presence rule. Document it with a Consular Report of Birth Abroad.

other: Married parents, one US citizen and one foreign (child born on or after Nov. 14, 1986): citizen parent needs 5 years of US presence, 2 of them after age 14.
Same case for children born Dec. 24, 1952 to Nov. 13, 1986: 10 years of presence, 5 after age 14.
At least one parent must be genetically or gestationally related to the child, and both must show a parental role.
Unmarried parents have separate rules for citizen mothers and fathers. See the State Dept page.
Whether the rules extend beyond one generation was not confirmed here.

citizenship.note: The US does not require you to give up another citizenship.

sources.label: State Dept: Citizenship for a Child Born Abroad
